questions.q: What does a consistency check verify?
options: Whether a value matches the real-world fact it represents
Whether a value matches an expected format or data type
Whether the same fact agrees with itself across related columns or systems
Whether a value is missing from a required field
questions.explain: Consistency is about agreement between copies or representations of the same fact — not about truth (accuracy), format (validity), or presence (completeness).

questions.q: A customer's State column contains a valid two-letter code, but their ZipCode is actually located in a different state. What dimension does this violate?
options: Consistency
Uniqueness
Completeness
Timeliness
questions.explain: Both fields could individually be validly formatted, but they disagree with each other — an internal consistency problem between two related columns in the same row.

questions.q: What is the difference between internal consistency and cross-system consistency?
options: They are the same check performed on different days
Internal consistency only applies to numeric data; cross-system only applies to text
Internal consistency requires a linked server; cross-system never does
Internal consistency compares columns within one row/table; cross-system consistency compares the same fact across two different systems
questions.explain: Internal consistency checks agreement between related columns in the same table (like OrderDate vs. SignupDate); cross-system consistency checks whether the same fact, stored independently in two systems, still agrees.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a consistency check's SQL can look nearly identical to an accuracy check's SQL, yet mean something different?
options: There is no real difference — the two terms are interchangeable
Consistency checks can only run on a single table, unlike accuracy checks
Consistency checks never use JOINs while accuracy checks always do
A consistency check only shows that two values disagree, not which one is actually correct
questions.explain: An accuracy check compares against a trusted, known-correct reference, so a mismatch means the checked value is wrong. A consistency check compares two independent systems of record, so a mismatch only reveals disagreement — resolving which side is correct is a separate step.

questions.q: Which example from the lesson illustrates an internal consistency check?
options: Flagging rows where a NOT NULL column contains an empty string
Flagging customers whose CRM email differs from their billing system email
Flagging duplicate CustomerId values within the same table
Flagging orders where OrderDate is earlier than the same customer's SignupDate
questions.explain: Comparing OrderDate to SignupDate within the same row/table is an internal consistency check. Comparing CRM to billing data is cross-system consistency, not internal.
